title: Deliverance from Necessity and the Broad Place
english: He is ransomed by God, being made outside of all disturbance. Thus the God of truth ransoms from deception; since God is the God of truth, He ransoms from deception and false glory. When someone has mistaken and false opinions, he cries out to God, so that by His truth He might make him outside of all deception. Again, the God of righteousness rescues from unrighteousnesses; for it is said: 'Hear me, O God of my righteousness' (Ps 25:1), so that you might make me outside of all unrighteousness, so that you might bring low those who work unrighteousness against me. And so it is for each one: Joseph called upon the God of self-control, so that he would not fall into the snares of the rebellious toward incontinence; and Susanna, so that she would not fall to the elders toward adultery. The God of self-control hears, not that He is another and another.

You hated those who guard vanities for nothing. Since you are the God of truth, and you hated those who guard vanities for nothing. But vanities are not true. And he said 'for nothing' because in a certain way they do not exist. Every falsehood is unsubstantial. Concerning the one who conceived the temple of Jesus, when I say 'she has brought forth' (τέτοκεν), I speak truly; but if I say, 'she has brought forth from a man,' I lie; it is not that she has brought forth, but the lie occurs regarding the manner. Every evil happens for nothing, it has no end. Therefore he says: You, O God, hated those who guard vanities for nothing. If anyone among those guarding such things receives understanding, who is the one hating such things, will he cease or will he hate himself?

But I have hoped in the Lord (Ps 118:49). You, O Master, did not 'hate those who guard vanities for nothing,' but I have hoped in you as my Lord; for it was possible to say, 'But I have hoped in you.' Instead he says, 'I have hoped in the Lord.' He speaks these things as a slave. From the disposition of a slave and the work of a slave he speaks these things.

I will rejoice and be glad in your mercy (Ps 118:54). Upon your mercy; for even if I confess you as Lord and I have hoped in you, it is not by my own power that the end is achieved, but by your mercy. For you have seen my lowliness (Ps 118:6). You have seen my lowliness which is about to receive [mercy]. Forgiving, you will not let me fall into it. You saved my soul from necessities. More simply in the Scripture, necessities are called tribulations; 'he...

For it is said, 'he will be brought out from necessity,' and, 'they cried to the Lord, and he heard them, and from their necessities he saved them.' He has brought [me] out from all tribulation, making it evident by his answering the plea; for a prayer was sent up, so that I might be rescued from enemies, from the impending wars.

It is possible, in a more logical way, to speak of the necessities of evil. Out of necessity, the evil man does not receive righteousness. I do not say that the man is not receptive to righteousness, but the unrighteous [man]. It is not that the outward state of the afflicted becomes [different], but that they are not defeated; for thus we also heard: 'save us from the evil one' (Matt 6:13), and 'do not bring us into temptation' (Matt 6:13). And if the apostles of Christ and the other righteous ones were pleading this, that they might not be tempted, they were never heard, if they are telling the truth saying: 'in everything we are afflicted, but not crushed' (2 Cor 4:8).

'And you did not shut me up in the hands of an enemy.' I am shut up in the hands of those attacking, when I am defeated by necessities and tribulations. But when I am saved from them, I am not shut up in their hands, nor do I do what they want to bring upon me. 'You have set my feet in a broad place.' This too must be understood in two ways. The movement according to the surrounding place, and that which is called broad and spacious according to evil.

It is a great thing having happened in this broad place and spaciousness: not to be dragged under, but to stand. And standing comes from God. Therefore he says gratefully: 'You have set my feet in a broad place.' My feet do not feel the tribulation surrounding [me]. For those saying: 'who shall separate us from the love of God? tribulation, distress' (Rom 8:35), they will say: 'You have set our feet in a broad place.' Even if the place in which we have come to be, and the road in which we find ourselves, is narrow, we see it as broad, you widening the tribulation. You provide a wider road of tribulation by helping.

'Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am afflicted.' But you say—and indeed you said: 'You have set my feet in a broad place'—so that the saint may pray unceasingly; for there is not one tribulation, for there is not one crisis in life, for there is not one temptation. If anyone, having pleaded, is rescued from one thing or from some people, he again sees others attacking, and again prays concerning those; for they afflict him...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unity of the Soul's Attributes
english: Things are expected. Or, does the prophet foresee them in advance? Such things even a prophet is not able to foresee. I am in a place where many are evil. They hate the righteous one who is there. Even if they once attack and bring a net or a snare and someone comes out of it, knowing their subsequent evil, he remains wide awake expecting such a thing again; 'for not indeed,' he says, 'will they sleep, unless they do evil; their sleep is taken away and they do not sleep' (Ps 31:3). And having been rescued many times, he also prays concerning the following.

My eye was greatly troubled in anger (Ps 32:3). My mind was troubled not in my own anger, but in the anger of the enemies or in your anger; for thinking against those committing sin, having sinned, I fell to the anger and my mind was troubled. My soul and my stomach (Ps 32:4). Not alone, he says, my eye—that is, the mind—was troubled by anger. And this is also possible: 'in anger my eye was troubled.' When I rage, my mind is disturbed; for the passions are disturbances of the mind. And my soul was troubled, of which the eye is the one troubled by the anger.

And 'my stomach'; he does not mean here the stomach of the body, but that which was receiving from the bridegroom and bringing forth: 'from your fear we have taken in in the stomach and labored' (Ps 31:7), so as to no longer save what was received, but to cast it away as small things. And this is also possible: because making the stomach calm, I did not receive the bread of heaven, but I received some other food, harmful, a poison, and my stomach has been disturbed. Therefore, he does not cast away salvation.

Or, the soul being disturbed? Some wish to say that the soul is threefold; rather, they say it is thick and divided. And they call the rational part of it the mind; for this is receptive of knowledge, and this is able to have knowledge. The desiring part does not receive knowledge, but sometimes is persuaded by the rational; being persuaded, it does not itself have knowledge. And just as when the winds of the air blow well, it becomes possible for the pilot—the ship not having such motion, but not opposing the skill of the winds not being contrary—and the desiring part again is persuaded by the rational, not having a calculation itself. Therefore, no one would be saying the mind while sinning. But all things together...

The soul is a single thing. Let us take an example. One takes a flower. The flower has such a color, but the color is not the flower itself. It also has such a fragrance, but the fragrance is not the flower. It also has such a shape. Therefore, all these things taken together are the flower. So when we say, 'The flower is fragrant' (Ps 143:6), we signify only one part of it, namely that it emits a sweet breath. And again, if we say it is bitter, we signify not only its juice alone. But the juice is not the flower; rather, all these things together are the flower.

Thus, when speaking about his own intellect or his own mind, saying that it is troubled by passion, the soul also says this. You know that when the helmsman is badly dragged, the whole vessel is damaged, and when the pilot is overturned, the ship is overturned. Therefore, the one called 'eye' is a certain intellectual power that steers the whole soul. If this is troubled, the soul is also disturbed.

And what about the generative womb? —which I have said many times, and now I will say: regarding sensible things, each thing is a specific kind and cannot be something else. A plant cannot be gold, and gold cannot be a man. But regarding intelligible things, it is possible through various relations and thoughts. For instance, I was saying yesterday that when the soul seeks, and seeks indeed to know itself, it possesses the word of both the seeker and the thing sought. And if it cultivates itself like a plant, the plant is not something else and the farmer is not someone else; difference is found in thought alone.

Therefore, if he says 'eye' and 'womb', it is possible to speak of both regarding the same power; because the mind is called an eye because it sees, and the womb is called a womb because it can generate and bring thoughts into the midst. 'For my life has wasted away in pain, and my years in lamentation' (Ps 102:9). Since my life has wasted away in pain—for I always had it painful—I sometimes lament and sometimes not; I always lament, desiring virtue; I always toil, I always sweat for the sake of the acquisition of the good. Since I suffer this through life, in a way my life has wasted away in pain and my years in lamentation; therefore I beseech you, so that I may no longer endure so much toil; for if I toil again guarding it, it is not the same toil as that of acquiring something and guarding what already exists. And what about how they are kinds in general? —if one requires the word of a man, not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Scorn of Enemies and Neighbors
english: He gives the Socrates example: do not say, 'Bring it, Dion.' The definition is, 'a mortal being is a rational animal.' And if I say, for instance, that the righteous man is outside of injustice, I am not speaking of this specific righteous man, but of the righteous man in general. For indeed the beginning of the psalm has become thus: 'In you, Lord, I have hoped, let me not be put to shame for ever' (Ps 25:2), regarding everyone who has hoped and is seeking an unashamed end of expectation; all the words take hold of this. For he who speaks in praise does not speak of this one or that one.

11 And my strength has grown weak in poverty, and my bones have been shaken. Here, poverty does not mean the deprivation of material goods. Strength here is spoken of in distinction of weakness. The strength which consists according to the soul is from wealth, but the sensory and bodily [strength] is not necessarily so; there are strong ones possessing nothing, and weak ones being masters of many goods. Just as if someone were to speak also concerning virtue or knowledge: 'Since I have fallen into poverty from virtue and knowledge, my strength, which I ought to have had from the presence of these qualities, has become weak.' 'My bones have been shaken.' Bones are parts of the body that hold the other parts together. While bones exist, nerves, veins, and the others can also be. Therefore, when the strong powers of the soul, called bones, become weak, the whole [soul] becomes in weakness.

And that he speaks of bones, not those of the body: 'All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?' (Ps 35:9); for the bones of the body do not have any concept of God, so that they might be able to say, whether there is anyone like Him or not. For it is necessary first to know God, and then thus to say. If therefore he says, 'All my bones shall say,' he means the powers of the soul which are well-proportioned and hold the other powers of it together, the sensory, the phantasic, the mnemonic. And again: 'My bones have been scattered by the netherworld,' those who confess and repent say. But regarding this netherworld, which is accustomed to be spoken of, the bones of the body cannot be scattered. And even if they were, as some say, under the moon, the bones of the dead do not undergo that. But when the powers of the soul, which through well-proportionedness are called bones, become [weak] by sin,

They were scattered like scorpions by the song, no longer preserving their own harmony. 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies and greatly to my neighbors' (Psalm 69:8). This psalm was said both before and in the presence of the Savior according to the man: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies.' It alludes to the cross; for he says in another psalm, which Paul took to be from the presence of the Savior: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (Psalm 41:9). I have received them. Some reproach you, O Father or O God, and these reproaches have fallen upon me. And it is nothing wonderful; often even a learned man, when he sees [others] mocking the learning, draws the reproaches upon himself. Those sinning are his enemies. This is said: 'For being enemies, we were estranged' (Psalm 51:11). The one sinning is an enemy of God, not God is an enemy of him; for God is an enemy to no one.

'And greatly to my neighbors' (Psalm 69:8). His neighbors are those promising to know his Scripture and calling themselves his partakers. Therefore, 'greatly': for example, let the Gentiles be enemies; for they sin and act impiously. I have become a reproach among all those, as having endured the cross, as having descended into death. 'And greatly to my neighbors.' But when those owing to me and promising to have their own buildings near me do the same things to enemies, the reproach among these has become great.

And a fear to those known to me. Those knowing me, having seen me suffering these things, had either a similar reverence, or had a fear of not suffering the same things. Those seeing me fled away from me. Those seeing me, having seen these things happening concerning me before, were seeing from outside me, not having departed from me, but they fled outside. Everyone fleeing Jesus becomes outside of him, outside of salvation. I was cast out as if dead from the heart. The enemies reproaching me, and the neighbors having done this greatly, cast me out from their hearts. And of the dead, a quick forgetting happens. For those undergoing afflictions say thus: 'From where the dead was placed, it is blotted out,' it says, 'the sorrow is blotted out from the soul.' They hasten...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
